message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
Here is what I recall, section by section. One caveat: the earlier text is still in my context, so I can't truly avoid "looking back" the way a person could. I've written this out without re-checking it against the original, so the wording is paraphrased and details may be slightly off.

**Title and opening**
- Title: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- A claim's weight comes partly from the evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they have already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common:
  - Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected.
  - Understating is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take the report as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding to anything, take it in and show you have.
- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This is not politeness; it keeps the conversation moving rather than circling.
- Start from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask.
- Then move: the restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms the direction, picks up the points you can act on, and says the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Return to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks.
- Re-deriving duplicates work and can signal distrust.
- The value of a shared record is that the team builds on it together.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into private versions of the truth and stops being able to act.
- Example: a report is summarised in the team notes as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Mark which questions are settled and which are less certain, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited later, whereas a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safe, is more common in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see material differently. That is valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer who starts from scratch rediscovers what the team already knows.
- So brief them: what you concluded, where you see risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- In reverse, as a new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- Check that your next step fits what the people who own the area have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release results when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked, which costs more than a short conversation would have.
- Your view comes from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't, and asking is how you learn them.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small, routine steps need no sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first, then act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether and how they'd like it restructured.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other. The pairs:
  - Overclaiming / second-guessing.
  - Inventing a flaw to look rigorous / overlooking a real one.
  - Closing too early / keeping open too long, including refusing to accept the team's answer.
  - Abandoning a line at the first difficulty / relitigating a decided one.
  - Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively, including disputing what experienced colleagues concluded.
  - Acting alone, making calls others should have shaped / waiting too long, delaying steps already agreed.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- This is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."
